title: Does Cough Syrup Have Alcohol? Robitussin, NyQuil and More
excerpt: Which cough syrups contain alcohol and how much: NyQuil, Robitussin, Delsym, DayQuil, Mucinex and prescription syrups, how to read the label, and who should avoid it.
metaDescription: Which cough syrups contain alcohol? NyQuil, Robitussin, Delsym and prescription syrups compared, how to check the label, and who should avoid it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** some cough syrups contain alcohol, but most of the ones on a US pharmacy shelf today don't. The best-known exception is the original Vicks NyQuil liquid, which lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient at 10%. Robitussin, Delsym, DayQuil, Mucinex liquids, children's cough products, and nearly every tablet, caplet and softgel are generally made without alcohol. A few prescription cough syrups, including common generic promethazine with codeine, do contain a small amount. When alcohol is in a liquid medicine, it's there to keep the active ingredients dissolved, not to make you sleepy, and the amount in one dose is small: roughly a sixth of a standard drink for a full dose of original NyQuil.

**The quick rules:** To find out whether your bottle has alcohol, read the "Inactive ingredients" line in the Drug Facts box, or look for "alcohol free" on the front of the package. If you take disulfiram (Antabuse) or metronidazole, are giving medicine to a child, or are about to take an alcohol test, choose an alcohol-free product and tell your pharmacist. And remember that "alcohol-free" only describes what's in the bottle. It doesn't make a cough medicine safe to take after you've been drinking, because the active ingredients still interact with the alcohol already in your system.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains what is printed on US over-the-counter labels and what's generally known about these ingredients. Formulas change, and store brands vary, so the label on the bottle in your hand is the final word. **Talk to a pharmacist or doctor before choosing a cough medicine if** you take disulfiram, metronidazole, tinidazole, a sedative, an antidepressant, an opioid, or any other prescription drug; you have liver disease; you're pregnant or breastfeeding; or you're buying for a child. **Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US), or 911 in an emergency, if** a child swallowed a cough or cold medicine that wasn't meant for them, or if someone who mixed cough medicine and alcohol is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, confused, or having a seizure.

## Why Some Cough Syrups Contain Alcohol at All

Liquid medicines have a practical problem: many active ingredients don't dissolve well in water. Manufacturers use a few tricks to keep them evenly mixed so that every spoonful contains the same dose. Alcohol (ethanol) is one of the oldest and cheapest of those tricks. It works as a **solvent**, helping drugs and flavorings dissolve, and as a **preservative**, helping stop bacteria and mold from growing in the bottle after you open it.

That's why you'll see alcohol listed under "Inactive ingredients" rather than "Active ingredients." It isn't there to treat your cough, and at a normal dose it isn't what makes a night-time syrup sleepy. That job belongs to the sedating antihistamine (more on that below).

Alcohol in cough syrup used to be much more common. Older cough and cold liquids, and especially products labeled as an **"elixir,"** often contained a lot more alcohol than anything you'll find today. Over the past few decades, pediatric groups raised concerns about alcohol in children's medicines, US regulators set limits, and manufacturers learned to use other solvents such as glycerin, propylene glycol and sorbitol. Most brands now advertise "alcohol free" as a selling point.

## Does Cough Syrup Have Alcohol? A Product-by-Product Look

This table is a starting point built from US product labels. It's meant to help you know what to check, not to replace the label. Brands reformulate, there are many versions of each product, and store brands differ, so always confirm on the "Inactive ingredients" line of the box you're holding.

| Product | Alcohol in the formula? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Vicks NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid (original) | Yes, listed at 10% | The best-known cough and cold liquid that still contains alcohol |
| Vicks NyQuil Alcohol Free liquid | No, labeled "Alcohol Free" | Same type of active ingredients as the original, minus the alcohol |
| NyQuil LiquiCaps | No drinking alcohol in the formula | Capsules are the simplest way to skip it |
| Vicks DayQuil liquid and LiquiCaps | Generally made without alcohol | Contains acetaminophen, so count it toward your daily limit |
| Robitussin cough syrups (adult) | Generally made without alcohol | Many Robitussin products say "alcohol-free" on the label |
| Delsym 12-hour cough liquid | Generally made without alcohol | Check the inactive ingredients on your specific version |
| Mucinex liquids and Mucinex DM | Generally made without alcohol | Plain Mucinex tablets contain no alcohol |
| Children's cough and cold liquids | Generally made without alcohol | US children's products are formulated alcohol-free; follow age limits |
| Store brands (CVS Health, Walgreens, Equate, Up & Up) | Varies by product | Many copy the brand they imitate, including "original" vs "alcohol free" versions |
| Promethazine with codeine (prescription, generic) | Yes, small amount (about 7% on common generic labels) | Never mix with drinking; opioid plus alcohol can slow breathing |
| Other prescription cough syrups | Varies | Ask the pharmacist, who can see the exact formulation |
| Products labeled "elixir" | Often yes | "Elixir" traditionally means a sweetened liquid that contains alcohol |
| Tablets, caplets, softgels, lozenges | Almost never | Solid forms don't need alcohol as a solvent |

Two things jump out from that table. First, original NyQuil is the main over-the-counter cough and cold liquid most people will run into that still contains alcohol. Second, if you want to be certain, switching from a liquid to a tablet or capsule almost always solves the problem.

## Does Robitussin Have Alcohol?

Current US Robitussin cough syrups for adults are generally made without alcohol, and many of them say "alcohol-free" on the box. Robitussin's active ingredients are typically dextromethorphan (a cough suppressant, the "DM" in the name), guaifenesin (an expectorant that thins mucus), or both, sometimes with other ingredients added in "multi-symptom" versions. Older Robitussin formulas and some international versions have contained alcohol, so if you're using an old bottle from the back of the cupboard or one bought abroad, read the label.

Alcohol-free doesn't mean it's fine to drink on it, though. Dextromethorphan can cause dizziness and drowsiness by itself, and alcohol makes those effects stronger. Our [cough medicine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) goes through Robitussin and Mucinex DM ingredient by ingredient.

## Does NyQuil Have Alcohol?

Yes, the original Vicks NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid does. It lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient at 10%. Vicks also sells a **NyQuil Alcohol Free** liquid, and the NyQuil LiquiCaps don't use drinking alcohol in the formula. NyQuil was originally much stronger in alcohol when it launched in the 1960s, and the amount was reduced over time.

Here's what 10% means in a real dose. This is simple arithmetic, not a lab measurement:

- An adult dose of NyQuil liquid is 30 mL (two tablespoons).
- Ten percent of 30 mL is about **3 mL of pure alcohol**.
- Alcohol weighs about 0.79 grams per mL, so that's roughly **2.4 grams**.
- A US standard drink contains about **14 grams** of alcohol.

So one dose of original NyQuil contains about a sixth of a standard drink. That's less than a couple of sips of wine. It's not enough to make a healthy adult drunk, and it isn't the main reason NyQuil and alcohol don't mix. The bigger problem is the sedating antihistamine and the acetaminophen inside it. For the full picture, see our [NyQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol).

## Does Delsym, DayQuil, or Mucinex Have Alcohol?

These are the other cough products people most often ask about:

- **Delsym** (extended-release dextromethorphan) liquids are generally made without alcohol. There are several Delsym versions, including children's and "cough plus" products, so check the inactive ingredients on yours.
- **DayQuil** liquid and LiquiCaps are generally made without alcohol. They're not sedating like NyQuil, but most versions contain acetaminophen, so the liver warning still applies if you drink. Our [DayQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) covers that in detail.
- **Mucinex** tablets contain no alcohol, and Mucinex liquids are generally made without it. Plain guaifenesin has no well-documented dangerous interaction with alcohol, but Mucinex DM, Fast-Max and night-time versions add other ingredients. See our [Mucinex and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/mucinex-and-alcohol).

## How to Tell If Your Cough Syrup Has Alcohol

You don't need to guess or search online every time. The answer is on the package.

1. **Look at the front of the box.** Products made without alcohol often say "alcohol free" right there, because it's a selling point.
2. **Find the Drug Facts panel.** It's on the back or side of every US over-the-counter medicine.
3. **Read the "Inactive ingredients" line, not just the active ones.** Alcohol is almost always an inactive ingredient. It may be listed as "alcohol," "ethanol," or "ethyl alcohol," sometimes with a percentage after it.
4. **Check for an alcohol percentage elsewhere on the label.** Some products state the alcohol content separately near the product name or net contents.
5. **Ask the pharmacist about prescription syrups.** Prescription bottles often don't come with the same consumer-friendly packaging. The pharmacist can look up the exact formulation in seconds.

A few words that look similar but are **not** drinking alcohol:

- **Benzyl alcohol** is a preservative used in small amounts. It's a different chemical from the ethanol in drinks.
- **Sugar alcohols** such as sorbitol, xylitol and maltitol are sweeteners. They don't contain ethanol and won't cause intoxication, though large amounts can upset your stomach.
- **Propylene glycol and glycerin** are common alcohol substitutes in liquid medicines. They're not ethanol either.

These matter if you're scanning a label quickly. "Alcohol" on its own, or "ethanol," is the one you're looking for.

## Rules for Alcohol in Children's Cough Medicine

US regulators have limited alcohol in over-the-counter medicines that are swallowed. Under the FDA's rule for these products (21 CFR Part 328), the allowed maximum depends on the age the product is meant for, with much lower limits for younger children and products for children under 6 required to be essentially alcohol-free. In practice, children's cough and cold liquids sold in the US today are generally made without alcohol.

The bigger safety issue for kids isn't the alcohol content. It's using the right product at all:

- Many cough and cold medicines aren't meant for young children. Follow the age limits on the label exactly.
- Use the measuring cup or syringe that comes with the product, not a kitchen spoon.
- Keep adult products, especially original NyQuil, out of reach. Young children are far more sensitive to alcohol than adults, and swallowing a lot of any adult medicine is a poisoning emergency regardless of its alcohol content.

If a child swallows medicine that wasn't meant for them, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they seem fine.

## Who Needs to Care About Alcohol in Cough Syrup

For most healthy adults, the small amount of alcohol in a dose of cough syrup isn't a medical problem. These are the situations where it's worth taking an extra minute at the shelf:

- **You take disulfiram (Antabuse).** Disulfiram causes a strong reaction (flushing, a pounding heart, nausea, vomiting) when it meets alcohol, and its prescribing information specifically warns against hidden sources such as cough syrups and other liquid medicines. Even small amounts can set it off. Ask your pharmacist to check every liquid you buy.
- **You take metronidazole or tinidazole.** These antibiotics carry warnings to avoid alcohol during treatment and for a period afterward. Our [metronidazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) explains the timing.
- **You're about to take an alcohol test.** Liquid medicine with alcohol can leave alcohol in your mouth for a short time, which can affect a breath test taken right away. That's one reason breath-test procedures usually include a waiting period of about 15 to 20 minutes before testing. Sensitive urine tests that look for alcohol breakdown products, such as EtG tests, can pick up small exposures, and US federal guidance on these tests has flagged incidental sources like medicines and mouthwash. If you're being tested, use an alcohol-free product and tell the tester what you've taken. Our guides to [how long alcohol stays on your breath](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-on-your-breath) and [how long alcohol stays in your urine](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-urine) explain the testing windows.
- **You're pregnant or breastfeeding.** The amount is small, but many people prefer to avoid it entirely. Several active ingredients in multi-symptom products also aren't recommended in pregnancy without advice, so ask your doctor or pharmacist.
- **You don't drink for religious, personal, or health reasons.** That's reason enough to read the label and choose an alcohol-free version or a tablet.
- **You're buying for a child.** Choose a product made for the child's age, and check the label.

## Can Cough Syrup Get You Drunk?

Not from the alcohol, at the labeled dose. A dose of original NyQuil contains about a sixth of a standard drink, and most cough syrups contain none at all. You'd have to drink a dangerous amount of medicine to get a meaningful amount of alcohol, and long before that, the active ingredients would make you seriously ill. Drinking large amounts of a product that contains acetaminophen can cause severe liver damage.

When cough syrup makes people feel "drunk" or out of it, the cause is the active ingredients, not alcohol:

- **Dextromethorphan (DXM)** is safe at the labeled dose but causes dizziness, confusion and hallucinations at high doses. Taking large amounts on purpose is dangerous, and combining it with alcohol makes it worse.
- **Sedating antihistamines** like doxylamine and diphenhydramine make people drowsy and clumsy, and alcohol stacks on top of that.
- **Codeine and other opioids** in prescription syrups can cause sleepiness and slowed breathing. Mixing them with alcohol, or with soda and candy as in the drink known as "lean," can be deadly.

If someone has taken a large amount of cough medicine, with or without alcohol, and is very drowsy, confused, vomiting, breathing slowly, or having a seizure, call 911. For questions about how much is too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

## Alcohol-Free Doesn't Mean Safe With Alcohol

This is the most common misunderstanding, and it's worth saying plainly. People often search "does cough syrup have alcohol" because they've been drinking and want something that won't "add more." But the alcohol inside a cough syrup is a small part of the story. The active ingredients are the real issue, and they're the same in the alcohol-free versions.

Here's how the main ingredients interact with drinks already in your system:

| Active ingredient | Found in | What happens with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Dextromethorphan (DXM) | Robitussin DM, Mucinex DM, Delsym, NyQuil, DayQuil | More dizziness, drowsiness and clumsiness |
| Doxylamine or diphenhydramine | NyQuil, most "PM" and night-time formulas | Strong sedative stacking; in a heavy drinker it can slow breathing |
| Acetaminophen | NyQuil and DayQuil Cold & Flu, many multi-symptom products | Extra strain on the liver; label warns people who have 3+ drinks a day |
| Guaifenesin | Plain Mucinex, Robitussin chest congestion | No well-documented dangerous interaction, but don't treat that as a green light |
| Codeine, hydrocodone | Prescription cough syrups | Dangerous; can slow or stop breathing. Never combine |

Sedating antihistamines and alcohol both slow the brain, but through different routes. The antihistamine blocks histamine, one of the brain chemicals that keeps you awake, while alcohol boosts GABA, the brain's main calming signal. Taking both is like pressing two different brakes at once, and the combined effect can be stronger than either alone.

Acetaminophen has a separate problem. Your liver turns a small part of each dose into a toxic by-product, and regular heavy drinking makes it harder for the liver to clear that by-product safely. That's why the US label warns that severe liver damage may occur in people who have 3 or more drinks every day while using it. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the chemistry.

If you've been drinking tonight, the safest move is to skip the cough medicine until you're sober, sip water or warm tea with honey for your throat, and take your medicine in the morning. For help choosing a product that fits your situation, see our [guide to alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine).

## Should You Use Cough Syrup for a Hangover?

No. Cough medicine doesn't treat any of the things that make a hangover miserable, such as dehydration, poor sleep, an irritated stomach, and the after-effects of your body processing alcohol. Night-time formulas add a sedative to a body that's already groggy, and acetaminophen-containing ones add work for your liver at a bad time. There is no good evidence that any cough syrup helps a hangover.

What does help is less exciting: water and electrolytes, food that's easy on the stomach, sleep, and time. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and if your throat is sore after a night of shouting over loud music, warm drinks and honey are a gentle place to start.

## A Note on DHM and Supplements

If you're reading labels this carefully, you probably care about what you put in your body, and you may have come across DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound sold as a supplement for people who drink. Here's an honest summary. Most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and may support the liver. Human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it does **not** change any of the medication advice on this page. It doesn't make it safe to combine cough medicine with alcohol, and it doesn't protect against acetaminophen overdose.

If you decide to try it on nights you drink (not on nights you're taking cough or cold medicine), a widely used option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and a higher-priced pick with added ingredients is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). If you take any prescription medicine, ask your pharmacist first. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what to check before combining it with other medicines.

## The Bottom Line

- **Most cough syrups sold in the US today don't contain alcohol.** Robitussin, Delsym, DayQuil, Mucinex liquids and children's products are generally made without it.
- **Original NyQuil liquid is the main exception**, at 10% alcohol, which works out to about a sixth of a standard drink per adult dose. Alcohol-free NyQuil and NyQuil LiquiCaps avoid it.
- **Some prescription cough syrups contain alcohol**, including common generic promethazine with codeine. These should never be combined with drinking.
- **Check the "Inactive ingredients" line** in the Drug Facts box, or switch to a tablet or capsule if you want to be sure.
- **Alcohol-free doesn't mean safe with alcohol.** The active ingredients are what interact with drinks already in your system.
- If you take disulfiram or metronidazole, are being tested for alcohol, are pregnant, or are buying for a child, choose an alcohol-free product and ask a pharmacist.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does cough syrup have alcohol in it?**

Some does, but most cough syrups sold in the US today don't. Original Vicks NyQuil liquid lists alcohol at 10% as an inactive ingredient, and some prescription syrups, such as generic promethazine with codeine, contain a small amount. Robitussin, Delsym, DayQuil, Mucinex liquids and children's cough products are generally made without alcohol. Check the "Inactive ingredients" line in the Drug Facts box to be sure.

**Does Robitussin have alcohol?**

Current US Robitussin cough syrups for adults are generally made without alcohol, and many say "alcohol-free" on the box. Older bottles and some international versions have contained alcohol, so check the label on yours. Even alcohol-free Robitussin DM shouldn't be combined with drinking, because dextromethorphan adds to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness.

**How much alcohol is in NyQuil?**

Original NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid lists alcohol at 10%. A 30 mL adult dose therefore contains about 3 mL of alcohol, roughly 2.4 grams, which is about a sixth of a US standard drink. NyQuil Alcohol Free liquid and NyQuil LiquiCaps don't contain drinking alcohol in the formula.

**Can cough syrup make you fail a breathalyzer or alcohol test?**

A dose of a liquid medicine that contains alcohol can leave alcohol in your mouth for a short time and affect a breath test taken right away, which is one reason testing procedures include a waiting period. Sensitive urine tests for alcohol breakdown products, such as EtG tests, can pick up small exposures. If you're subject to testing, use an alcohol-free product and tell the tester what you've taken.

**Is there alcohol in children's cough syrup?**

Children's cough and cold liquids sold in the US today are generally made without alcohol, and federal rules sharply limit alcohol in medicines meant for children. Many cough and cold products aren't meant for young children at all, so follow the age limits on the label and ask a pediatrician or pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Can I take cough syrup if I'm on Antabuse or metronidazole?**

Ask your pharmacist before taking any liquid medicine. Disulfiram (Antabuse) can cause a strong reaction to even small amounts of alcohol, and its prescribing information warns about hidden sources such as cough syrups. Metronidazole and tinidazole also carry alcohol warnings. Choose a product labeled alcohol-free or a tablet, and have the pharmacist confirm it.

**Is alcohol-free cough syrup safe to take after drinking?**

Not necessarily. "Alcohol-free" describes what's in the bottle, not how the medicine interacts with drinks already in your system. Dextromethorphan, sedating antihistamines and acetaminophen all interact with alcohol, whether or not the syrup itself contains any. The safest approach is to wait until you're sober before taking cough or cold medicine.

**Can you get drunk from cough syrup?**

Not from the alcohol at the labeled dose. Even original NyQuil contains only about a sixth of a standard drink per dose, and most cough syrups contain none. When people feel intoxicated from cough syrup, it's from taking large amounts of active ingredients such as dextromethorphan or codeine, which is dangerous. If someone is very drowsy, confused, or breathing slowly after taking a lot of cough medicine, call 911.
